title.en: Language work for How I Taught My Grandmother to Read: word pairs, prefixes, idioms and the past perfect
Words and sentences for a story about learning

text.en: In the story the writer teaches her grandmother to read, and the language work of the chapter helps us talk about learning. We study word pairs called binomials, prefixes that change meanings, idioms about studying, the difference between the simple past and the past perfect, and the format of a formal letter to the editor.

text.en:
A binomial is a pair of words joined by 'and' or 'or' that always appear in the same order, such as sink or swim, on and off, mix and match, all or nothing, part and parcel, pick and choose, sooner or later and by leaps and bounds.
Sink or swim means you must succeed by your own effort or fail. Part and parcel means an essential part of something. Pick and choose means to select carefully. Sooner or later means at some time in the future. By leaps and bounds means very fast progress.
A prefix is a group of letters placed before a word to change its meaning. The prefix un makes the opposite, as in unable and unhappy. Im also gives the opposite before p or m, as in impossible and immature.
Dis gives the opposite or removal, as in disagree and disappear. In gives the opposite, as in incorrect and inactive. Mis means wrongly, as in misunderstand and misspell. Extra means beyond, as in extraordinary and extracurricular.
The book also gives idioms about learning. To hit the books means to study hard. To draw a blank means to be unable to remember something. To learn the ropes means to learn how a job is done.
To rack one's brain means to think very hard. To learn by heart means to memorise something so well that you can repeat it exactly. To burn the midnight oil means to work or study late into the night.
The simple past tense talks about a finished action at a definite time in the past, as in 'The writer taught her grandmother every evening'.
The past perfect tense is made with had plus the third form of the verb. It shows the action that happened first when two past actions are told together. In 'When the teacher arrived, the lesson had started', the starting came first and the arriving came second.
To fill a blank, ask which action happened earlier. Put the past perfect for the earlier action and the simple past for the later one, as in 'She had finished her work before her friends came'.
A letter to the editor is a formal letter about a matter of public interest. It has the writer's name and address, the date, a subject of four or five words in title case, the salutation Sir or Madam, a body of at least three paragraphs and the close Yours truly.
In the body, the first paragraph states the problem and refers to a news item or an experience. The second paragraph explains the causes and the effects. The third paragraph offers solutions and asks the editor to publish the letter.
For the speaking activity in the book, you talk about a turncoat, a person who changes sides to suit their own gain, and use phrases such as 'I strongly believe' and 'to put it in a few words'. For the listening task on digital literacy, read the questions first and listen for the exact words.

problem.en: Complete the sentence with the correct tense: 'When I reached the station, the train ____ (leave).'

text.en: When I reached the station, the train had left.

why.en: The train left first, so the past perfect had left is used.

text.en: Add the prefix mis to the word 'spell'.

points.en: Binomials: sink or swim, part and parcel, pick and choose, sooner or later, by leaps and bounds.
Prefixes: un, im, dis, in, mis, extra.
Idioms: hit the books, draw a blank, learn the ropes, rack one's brain, learn by heart, burn the midnight oil.
Past perfect = had + past participle, for the earlier past action.
A letter to the editor has three paragraphs: problem, analysis, solution.
